passages.t: A man caught up to the third heaven
passages.happening:
Paul goes on with his foolish boasting, though he says there is nothing to gain by it. “I will go on to visions and revelations from the Lord” (verse 1).

He tells it strangely, as if about someone else. “I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven. Whether it was in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows” (verse 2).

He says it again: this man “was caught up to Paradise. The things he heard were too sacred for words, things that man is not permitted to tell” (verse 4).

Then he stops. He will boast about ‘such a man’, but about himself only in his weaknesses (verse 5). He could boast and still tell the truth. “But I refrain, so no one will credit me with more than he sees in me or hears from me” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Who was the man? Almost all readers agree that Paul means himself. Verse 7 makes it plain: the revelations were his, and so was the thorn that followed. He speaks of ‘a man in Christ’ to keep the honour away from himself. Even his greatest experience is something that happened to him, not something he achieved.

‘Fourteen years ago’ counts back from a letter written about AD 55 or 56. That puts the vision in the early 40s, give or take. Those were the years Paul spent in Syria and Cilicia (Galatians 1:21), about which we know very little. So this is not the Damascus road, which came earlier.

What did ‘the third heaven’ mean? Jewish writings from around Paul's time and later count the heavens in different ways: some speak of three, some of seven. One of them, known as 2 Enoch, whose date is debated, places paradise in the third heaven. Paul does not explain his picture. Most readers think ‘the third heaven’ and ‘Paradise’ name the same place: the very presence of God. Some think Paul describes two stages of one experience.

‘Paradise’ comes from an old Persian word for an enclosed garden or park. The old Greek translation used it for the garden of Eden. Later it named the place where the righteous are with God. Jesus promised the thief on the cross, “today you will be with Me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43).

The rival teachers seem to have boasted of visions. Paul has one greater than theirs, and he will not use it. He tells it in the third person, does not say what he saw, and will not say what he heard.
passages.ot:
The prophets had visions of God. Isaiah said, “I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted” (Isaiah 6:1). Ezekiel said, “the heavens opened and I saw visions of God” (Ezekiel 1:1). Yet even they described what they saw with great care, and much was left unsaid.

Paradise points back to the beginning: “And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east” (Genesis 2:8). Paul was taken, for a moment, to the place where people and God were first at home together.

Some things are not for telling. Moses said, “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever” (Deuteronomy 29:29). Daniel was told to “shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:4).
passages.hard:
What should we make of people today who say they have visited heaven?

Paul is our best guide. He had such an experience, and look at what he did with it. He waited fourteen years to mention it. He spoke of himself as ‘a man’. He did not know whether he had been in the body or out of it. He would not describe what he heard. And he did not build his teaching on it. He used it only to show that visions prove nothing, and then turned at once to his weakness.

Books and talks that describe heaven in detail, and are sold on that basis, are doing something very different. These notes do not judge anyone's private experience. People who have been near death sometimes report striking things, and God can do as he pleases. But no such account adds to what Scripture says, and Christians should not trust a teacher more because he claims to have seen heaven. Paul warned in another letter against anyone who would disqualify others “with speculation about what he has seen” (Colossians 2:18). The safe ground is what God has made known in Christ and in Scripture.
passages.asks: Paul had a great experience of God, and chose to say almost nothing about it. Ask what you are tempted to make much of in your own spiritual life, and why. Then ask whether your trust in God rests on unusual experiences, yours or other people's, or on what he has said and done in Christ.

passages.t: The thorn in the flesh: ‘My grace is sufficient for you’
passages.happening:
Paul now tells what came after the revelations. “So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me” (verse 7).

He prayed for it to go. “Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me” (verse 8).

The answer was no, and something better than yes. The Lord said to him, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (verse 9).

So Paul changed what he boasts of. “Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me” (verse 9). “That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
A ‘thorn’ is the Greek skolops. It means a sharp stake or a splinter. It comes only here in the New Testament. Whether small or large, it is something that pierces and keeps on hurting.

Notice that Paul says both things. The thorn was ‘given’ to keep him humble; most read that as God's purpose. And it was ‘a messenger of Satan, to torment me’. Paul does not explain how both are true. He does not call the pain good. He calls it a messenger of Satan. Yet he believes God was at work in it.

‘The Lord’ who answered is the risen Christ. These are the only words of the risen Jesus quoted in this letter. ‘Sufficient’ means ‘enough’. In Greek the verb is in the present tense: grace that is enough now, and goes on being enough.

‘Rest on me’ is, word for word, ‘spread a tent over me’. Some readers hear in it the picture of God's presence dwelling in the tabernacle. The power of Christ lives where Paul is weakest.
passages.ot:
The word ‘thorns’ in a person's side is used in the Law for enemies who would trouble Israel: “those you allow to remain will become barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides” (Numbers 33:55). That is one reason some readers think Paul's thorn was people who opposed him.

Job is the clearest Old Testament case of suffering that comes from Satan but is held within God's limits. “Very well,” said the LORD to Satan. “He is in your hands, but you must spare his life” (Job 2:6). Joseph said to his brothers, “As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20).

The psalms pray honestly for healing. “Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are in agony” (Psalm 6:2). And Isaiah says of God, “He gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the weak” (Isaiah 40:29).
passages.hard:
What was the thorn, and why did God not take it away?

No one knows what it was. Paul does not say, and every answer is a guess. Many think it was an illness. Some think of his eyes, because he told the Galatians, “it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you” (Galatians 4:13), and that they would have torn out their eyes for him (Galatians 4:15). Some think of a difficulty in speaking, since his critics said ‘his speaking is of no account’ (10:10). Others think it was persecution, or one person who kept opposing him, since ‘a messenger of Satan’ can be a person and Numbers uses ‘thorns’ for enemies. Some medieval readers took it as an inner temptation. The text does not let anyone decide. Perhaps that is a mercy, since people with many kinds of pain have found themselves in it.

Why was it not removed? Paul gives two reasons: to keep him from pride, and so that Christ's power would rest on him. Paul prayed three times. So did Jesus in Gethsemane, “Yet not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:39).

This is not a general rule that God will not heal. The New Testament tells of many healings, and Christians pray for the sick. Nor is it a reason to refuse a doctor or treatment. Paul called his friend Luke “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). It is one man's honest witness that God sometimes answers a prayer for relief with grace to bear it.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul asked three times for the thorn to go, and then heard ‘My grace is sufficient for you’. Ask what you have prayed for again and again. You are free to keep asking, as he did. And ask where, in your weakness, you have known God's grace to be enough for today.

passages.happening:
Paul ends the fool's speech. “I have become a fool, but you drove me to it” (verse 11). They should have spoken up for him, he says, “since I am in no way inferior to those” the church admired, ‘even though I am nothing’ (verse 11).

He reminds them what they saw. The true marks of an apostle, ‘signs, wonders, and miracles’, he says, “were performed among you with great perseverance” (verse 12).

Then a last piece of irony. “In what way were you inferior to the other churches, except that I was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong!” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Paul's ‘signs, wonders, and miracles’ are not described in the Acts account of his time in Corinth. But he speaks of them as things the Corinthians saw for themselves. He wrote the same to Rome, of what Christ had done through him “by the power of signs and wonders, and by the power of the Spirit of God” (Romans 15:19).

Note what Paul does not do. Even here he does not make the miracles his main proof. He says they were done ‘with great perseverance’, that is, in the middle of hardship. And he calls himself ‘nothing’.

His “Forgive me this wrong!” (verse 13) is irony. The only way he treated Corinth worse than other churches was by refusing to take their money. He asks pardon for having been generous.
passages.ot:
‘Signs and wonders’ is an Old Testament phrase for God's great acts at the exodus. Moses was the prophet “whom the LORD knew face to face” (Deuteronomy 34:10), and the next verse speaks of the signs and wonders the LORD sent him to do in Egypt (Deuteronomy 34:11).

Moses, for all his signs, is also remembered for humility: “Now Moses was a very humble man, more so than any man on the face of the earth” (Numbers 12:3). Power and humility belonged together in God's servant.
passages.asks: Paul's proof was what God had done among the Corinthians, not his own greatness. Ask what God has done in your life that you have forgotten to thank him for. And ask whether you have ever made someone feel small for their generosity, or failed to notice it.

passages.t: ‘I am not seeking your possessions, but you’
passages.happening:
Paul is ready to come a third time, and again he will not be a burden. “I am not seeking your possessions, but you. For children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children” (verse 14).

He will gladly give all he has. “And for the sake of your souls, I will most gladly spend my money and myself. If I love you more, will you love me less?” (verse 15).

Then he answers a charge. Some say that he did not take their money himself, but tricked them some other way (verse 16). So he asks: “Did I exploit you by anyone I sent you?” (verse 17). “Did Titus exploit you in any way? Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
‘This is the third time’ tells us there had been a second visit. Acts records only the first, when Paul founded the church. The second was the painful visit of 2:1.

Everyone in that world assumed that parents provide for children, not the other way round. Paul had called himself their father in the faith: “for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). So he will spend himself for them.

Verse 16 sounds strange: ‘crafty as I am, I caught you by trickery’. Paul is repeating what his critics said. The charge seems to have been that the collection for Jerusalem was a trick to get money into Paul's hands. That is why he took such care with it, as chapter 8 showed. He answers by pointing to Titus and the brother: they took nothing either.
passages.ot:
Proverbs takes it for granted that parents provide for their children: “A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children” (Proverbs 13:22).

Samuel, at the end of his long service, asked Israel to say if he had ever cheated them: “Whose ox or donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated or oppressed?” (1 Samuel 12:3). The people answered that he had not. Paul makes the same kind of appeal.
passages.asks: Paul wanted the Corinthians themselves, not what they owned. Ask whether there is someone you have treated as useful rather than loved. And ask what it would mean for you to spend yourself gladly for others, as a parent does for a child.

passages.happening:
Paul says this has not really been a defence of himself. “We speak before God in Christ, and all of this, beloved, is to build you up” (verse 19).

He tells them his fears. He may not find them as he hopes, and they may not find him as they hope. “I fear that there may be quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder” (verse 20).

And there is a deeper fear. “I am afraid that when I come again, my God will humble me before you, and I will be grieved over many who have sinned earlier and have not repented of their acts of impurity, sexual immorality, and debauchery” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The first list is about how people treat each other: quarrels, jealousy, anger, slander, gossip. These were the sins that had split the church from the start (1 Corinthians 1:11). The second list is about the body: impurity and sexual sin, as in 1 Corinthians 5 and 6. Paul names both together. No reader stands outside these lists.

Look at what Paul fears for himself. Not that he will be angry, but that God will ‘humble’ him, and that he will ‘grieve’. A father whose children are in trouble does not feel proud. He feels it. And Paul's hope is that they will repent before he comes, so that the visit can be a joy.
passages.ot:
The prophets grieved over the sins of God's people. Jeremiah said, “Oh, that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears! I would weep day and night over the slain daughter of my people” (Jeremiah 9:1).

And God's call to turn back is old. “Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness” (Jeremiah 3:22).
passages.asks: Paul named quarrels and gossip beside sexual sin. Ask which of the sins in verses 20 and 21 you are most likely to excuse in yourself. Then ask how you would want a visit from someone who loves you to go, and what you might put right before it comes.
